citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

Assume AC. Define $\gamma(E)=\int_E e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}\,dx$ for Borel E in $\mathbb R$. By The standard normal density has total mass one and The indefinite integral of a nonnegative measurable function is a measure, gamma is a probability measure; denote it $N(0,1)$. For $m\in\mathbb R$ and $\sigma\ge0$, define $N(m,\sigma^2)$ as the law of $x\mapsto m+\sigma x$ on $(\mathbb R,\mathcal B,\gamma)$. This affine map is continuous: for $\sigma$>0 choose $\delta$=$\varepsilon$/$\sigma$, and for $\sigma$=0 it is constant. Its inverse images of opens are open, so it is Borel measurable. The law of a random element is a probability measure makes its pushforward a probability. When $\sigma$=0, the preimage of E is all of R if m belongs to E and empty otherwise, so $N(m,0)=\delta_m$ in The Dirac set function at a point.

derivations.claim: Under [A1], the standard normal probability law of [F2] is supplied. Its density $\phi$ is positive and symmetric and integrates to one. Thus $\Phi$ is continuous and strictly increasing, $\Phi(0)=1/2$, and $\Phi(y)\to1$ as $y\to\infty$; the intermediate value theorem gives the unique $z>0$ with $\Phi(z)=0.975$.

The prior density times likelihood is proportional to $\exp\{-\tfrac12[\theta^2+(Y-\theta)^2]\}=\exp\{-(\theta-Y/2)^2\}$ times a factor independent of $\theta$. Normalization gives posterior law $N(Y/2,1/2)$.
Under the fixed truth $\theta_*=2r+1$, write $Y=\theta_*+Z$. The event $\theta_*\in I(Y)$ is equivalent to $|Z-\theta_*|\le2r$, hence to $1\le Z\le4r+1$.

The interval membership graph is $\{(Y,\theta):|\theta-Y/2|\le r\}$, the inverse image of the closed interval $[-r,r]$ under a continuous map. It is closed, hence Borel, so the sampling membership event is measurable.
Under that posterior, $(\theta-Y/2)/\sqrt{1/2}$ is standard normal. The interval radius $r=z/\sqrt2$ therefore gives posterior mass $\Phi(z)-\Phi(-z)=0.975-0.025=0.95$ for every observed $Y$.
Since the standard normal density is positive and symmetric, $P(1\le Z\le4r+1)<P(Z\ge0)=1/2<0.95$. Thus the interval has posterior mass $0.95$ but frequentist coverage below $0.95$ at $\theta_*$.

citations.quote:
The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Write $\mathbb N_+=\{1,2,\ldots\}$. Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. For $\beta>0$
and $M>0$, the **Gaussian-sequence hyperrectangle** of smoothness index
$\beta$ and radius $M$ is
$$\Theta_\beta(M):= \left\{\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N_+,\mathbb R): \sup_{i\ge1}i^{1+2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\right\}.$$
The definition uses a coordinatewise weighted bound. It is distinct from the
Sobolev ellipsoid $\{\theta:\sum_i i^{2\beta}\theta_i^2\le M\}$.

Let $\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ be the real square-summable sequence space
from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]]. Fix
$L_0\ge1$, an integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho\ge2$. The **polished-tail class**
$\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ consists of the sequences
$\theta\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$ such that for every integer
$N\ge N_0$,
$$\sum_{i=N}^{\infty}\theta_i^2 \le L_0\sum_{i=N}^{\lfloor\rho N\rfloor}\theta_i^2.$$
Thus each tail's total squared mass is controlled by the mass in the finite
block from $N$ through $\lfloor\rho N\rfloor$. The condition concerns block
energy; it is not a coordinatewise upper or lower bound.

The adaptive empirical-Bayes credible balls have nonvanishing frequentist
coverage uniformly over every truth in a hyperrectangle $\Theta_\beta(M)$.

**Explicit sparse-gap construction.**

Use [[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]], assume AC,
and fix $\beta>0$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$ and a finite
$A>\beta$. Run the procedure with the fixed cap $A_n=A$ and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Choose
$0<M\le(1984C^8)^{-1}$. Put $s=1+2\beta+2p$, $\rho_j=2^j$,
$n_1=2$, and
$$n_{j+1}=\left\lceil(2\rho_{j+1}^2)^s n_j\right\rceil,\qquad N_j=n_j^{1/s}.$$
Define the fixed nonnegative truth by
$$\theta_{0,i}^2=\begin{cases}0,&N_j/\rho_j<i\le N_j\text{ for some }j,\\0,&2N_j<i\le\rho_jN_j\text{ for some }j,\\Mi^{-1-2\beta},&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}$$
Then $\theta_{0,1}=0$ and $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$. For every
deterministic nonnegative inflation sequence for which there exist
$K_L\in(0,\infty)$ and $j_0\in\mathbb N$ such that, for every $j\ge j_0$,
$$L_{n_j}\le K_L\sqrt M\,\rho_j^{(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)}$$
one has
$$P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_{n_j}(L_{n_j})\}\longrightarrow0.$$
The finitely many indices with $n_j<3$ are irrelevant. In particular,
for every $\beta>0$ this gives a counterexample for any fixed cap
$A>\beta$, including constant inflation factors.

Use the Gaussian sequence procedure of
[[def-adaptive-empirical-bayes-gaussian-sequence-procedure]] with fixed
$p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $A>0$, and
$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}$. Fix $L_0\ge1$, $N_0\ge1$,
$\rho\ge2$, and $\gamma\in(0,1)$. Assume that
$\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)$ and
$\theta_{0,1}=0$. Then there is a finite inflation constant $L>0$,
depending only on the fixed model and class parameters, such that
$$\inf_{\substack{\theta_0\in\Theta_{\mathrm{pt}}(L_0,N_0,\rho)\\ \theta_{0,1}=0}} P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_n(L)\} \longrightarrow1.$$
This is conservative frequentist coverage tending to one, not exact
asymptotic coverage $1-\gamma$. The source also allows a sequence of caps
$A_n>0$ satisfying, for all sufficiently large $n$,
$$A_n\le \frac{\sqrt{\log n}}{4\sqrt{\log(\rho\vee e)}}.$$
In that case there is a constant $K_{\mathrm{infl}}>0$, depending only on the
fixed model and class parameters and not on $n$, such that the same coverage
conclusion holds for any deterministic inflation sequence satisfying
$$L_n\ge K_{\mathrm{infl}}(3\rho^{3(1+2p)})^{A_n}$$
for all sufficiently large $n$.

Assume AC. Fix $n\ge3$, $p\ge0$, $C\ge1$, $\gamma\in(0,1)$,
an inflation factor $L\ge0$, and a finite $A_n>0$. Let
$(\kappa_i)_{i\ge1}$ be known nonzero real numbers satisfying
$$C^{-2}i^{-2p}\le\kappa_i^2\le C^2i^{-2p}.$$
For a true parameter $\theta_0\in\ell^2(\mathbb N,\mathbb R)$, the observation
sequence is
$$X_i=\kappa_i\theta_{0,i}+n^{-1/2}Z_i,\qquad i\ge1,$$
where $(Z_i)_{i\ge1}$ are independent $N(0,1)$ random variables. The
corresponding sampling law is denoted $P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}$.

For $0<\alpha\le A_n$, let
$$\Pi_\alpha=\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,i^{-1-2\alpha}).$$
Its coordinate posterior rule is the product of
$$N\!\left(\widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x), v_{n,\alpha,i}\right),\qquad \widehat\theta_{n,\alpha,i}(x)= \frac{n\kappa_i x_i}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2},\qquad v_{n,\alpha,i}=\frac{1}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2}.$$
For $\alpha>0$, the marginal log likelihood relative to the reference law
$\bigotimes_{i\ge1}N(0,n^{-1})$ is
$$\ell_n(\alpha;x)=-\frac12\sum_{i=1}^{\infty} \left[ \log\!\left(1+\frac{n\kappa_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}}\right) -\frac{n^2\kappa_i^2x_i^2}{i^{1+2\alpha}+n\kappa_i^2} \right].$$
For maximization, use this same source score series at every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, with the sum taken in increasing coordinate order.
Choose a Borel data domain $D_n\subseteq\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}$ such that
the series converges to a finite value for every $x\in D_n$ and every
$\alpha\in[0,A_n]$, and $\alpha\mapsto\ell_n(\alpha;x)$ is upper
semicontinuous there. For each truth under consideration assume
$P_{\theta_0}^{(n)}(D_n)=1$. Also assume a Borel-measurable selector
$x\mapsto\widehat\alpha_n(x)$ on $D_n$ is supplied, with
$\widehat\alpha_n(x)\in\operatorname*{arg\,max}_{0\le\alpha\le A_n}
\ell_n(\alpha;x)$.
These domain, endpoint-score and selector conditions are explicit procedure
hypotheses; no arbitrary score value at $\alpha=0$ is added. At
$\widehat\alpha_n>0$, let $r_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n)$ be the
$1-\gamma$ quantile of the centered posterior $\ell^2$ norm and use the
posterior mean given above. Define the empirical-Bayes set by
$$\widehat C_n(L;x)= \begin{cases} \{\theta\in\ell^2: \|\theta-\widehat\theta_{n,\widehat\alpha_n(x)}(x)\|_2 \le Lr_{n,\gamma}(\widehat\alpha_n(x))\},& \widehat\alpha_n(x)>0,\\ \ell^2,&\widehat\alpha_n(x)=0. \end{cases}$$
Use the source convention $r_{n,\gamma}(0)=+\infty$ for the second branch;
no posterior probability on $\ell^2$ is asserted at $\alpha=0$. A separate
local lemma verifies the coordinate posterior and evidence formulas for
$\alpha>0$.

Let $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ be a measurable parameter space and, for each integer $n\ge1$, let $\mathcal E_n=((\mathsf Y_n,\mathcal Y_n),(P_{\theta,n})_{\theta\in\Theta})$ be a statistical experiment. Let $\Pi_{0,n}$ be a proper prior on $(\Theta,\mathcal T)$ and let $y\mapsto\Pi_n(\cdot\mid y)$ be a supplied posterior probability kernel under the associated prior-predictive law. For $0<\gamma<1$, a data-indexed set rule $C_n:\mathsf Y_n\to\mathcal P(\Theta)$ is a posterior credible set at level $1-\gamma$ if its membership graph $\{(y,\theta):\theta\in C_n(y)\}$ is in $\mathcal Y_n\otimes\mathcal T$ and $\Pi_n(C_n(y)\mid y)\ge1-\gamma$ for every $y$ in its declared data domain. At a fixed truth $\theta\in\Theta$, its frequentist coverage is $c_n(\theta):=P_{\theta,n}\{y:\theta\in C_n(y)\}$. For a truth class $\mathcal T_n\subseteq\Theta$, the rule is asymptotically honest at level $1-\gamma$ on $\mathcal T_n$ if $\liminf_{n\to\infty}\inf_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}c_n(\theta)\ge1-\gamma$, and it is asymptotically exactly calibrated there if $\sup_{\theta\in\mathcal T_n}|c_n(\theta)-(1-\gamma)|\to0$.

derivations.claim: Every squared coordinate is either zero or $Mi^{-1-2\beta}$, so $\sup_i i^{1+2\beta}\theta_{0,i}^2\le M$ and $\sum_i\theta_{0,i}^2\le M\sum_i i^{-1-2\beta}<\infty$. Also $N_1=2^{1/s}\in(1,2)$ and $\rho_1=2$, hence $N_1/\rho_1<1\le N_1$ and the first zero gap contains $i=1$. Thus $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$ and $\theta_{0,1}=0$.

Fix any polished-tail parameters $L_0\ge1$, integer $N_0\ge1$, and $\rho_*\ge2$. The recursion gives $N_j/\rho_j\ge2\rho_jN_{j-1}>\rho_{j-1}N_{j-1}$, so every earlier gap ends below $N_j/\rho_j$. Also $N'_j=\lfloor2N_j\rfloor+1\le2N_j+1$; because $N_j\to\infty$ and $\rho_j\to\infty$, for all sufficiently large $j$ we have $N'_j\ge N_0$ and $\rho_*(2N_j+1)\le\rho_jN_j$, whence $\lfloor\rho_*N'_j\rfloor\le\rho_jN_j$. Since $N'_j>2N_j$, the block $[N'_j,\lfloor\rho_*N'_j\rfloor]$ lies in the current zero gap $(2N_j,\rho_jN_j]$. For all sufficiently large $j$, $i_j=\lfloor\rho_jN_j\rfloor+1\le\rho_jN_j+1<4\rho_jN_j\le N_{j+1}/\rho_{j+1}$, so $i_j$ is before the next first gap; applying the same separation at later indices puts all still later gaps farther right. Since $\rho_jN_j>2N_j+1\ge N'_j$ eventually, $i_j>N'_j$; earlier gaps end below $N_j/\rho_j<i_j$. Hence $i_j$ lies outside every zero gap and is in the tail from $N'_j$, with $\theta_{0,i_j}^2=Mi_j^{-1-2\beta}>0$. The block sum is zero while that tail is positive, violating [F2]. Thus $\theta_0$ is outside every fixed polished-tail class.

For a fixed $L\ge1$, take $L_{n_j}=L$ and $K_L=L/\sqrt M$. Since $(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)>0$ and $\rho_j\ge1$, we have $L_{n_j}=L\le K_L\sqrt M\,\rho_j^{(1+2p)/(8+8\beta+8p)}$ for every $j$. Applying [F3] gives $P_{\theta_0}^{(n_j)}\{\theta_0\in\widehat C_{n_j}(L)\}\to0$. By [F6] this is the frequentist coverage at the fixed truth; because $\theta_0\in\Theta_\beta(M)$ by step 1.1, the infimum coverage over that hyperrectangle cannot have lower limit at least $1-\gamma$.

The positive coverage statement [F4] has the additional polished-tail hypothesis, which fails for $\theta_0$ by step 2.1. Thus the sparse-gap undercoverage does not contradict the polished-tail theorem; it refutes only the broader fixed-inflation claim over the full hyperrectangle.
